--- subtitle: "Chapter 1: Introduction and Course Recap" code-annotations: hover --- ## Basic information **Contact information** - email address: bertille.picard@ensai.fr - office: 254 - please send an email before

**Suggested textbooks** - Wooldridge, Jeffrey. 2018. Introductory Econometrics : A Modern Approach. 7th edition. Andover (GBR) ; Independence, KY. - Baltagi, Badi H. 2021. Econometric Analysis of Panel Data, 6th Edition. Vol. 4. Springer. # Theory ## Review of Data Types ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Cross-sectional data > Data collected at a single point in time from multiple subjects, such as individuals, households, firms, or countries. This type of data allows for comparisons between different subjects at the same time. > | **ID** | **Name** | **Employment Status** | **Year** | |--------|----------|-----------------------|----------| | 1 | Alice | Employed | 2023 | | 2 | Bob | Unemployed | 2023 | | 3 | Carol | Employed | 2023 | | 4 | Dave | Employed | 2023 | ### Repeated cross-sectional data >Results from collecting cross-sectional data at multiple time points. Although the data is collected at different times, the subjects observed are not necessarily the same across each time point, allowing for analysis of changes over time within the population. > | **ID** | **Name** | **Employment Status** | **Year** | |--------|----------|-----------------------|----------| | 1 | Alice | Employed | 2023 | | 2 | Bob | Unemployed | 2023 | | 3 | Dave | Employed | 2023 | | 4 | Eve | Employed | 2022 | | 5 | Frank | Unemployed | 2022 | | 6 | Henry | Unemployed | 2022 | ### Time series >Observations of the same variable recorded over a period of time, often at regular intervals. This type of data is used to analyze trends, cycles, and patterns over time within the same subject or entity. > | **Date** | **Unemployment Rate** | |------------|------------------------| | Jan 2020 | 8.0% | | Feb 2020 | 7.8% | | ... | ... | | Dec 2023 | 6.5% | ### 👉 Panel Data 👈 >Combines elements of both cross-sectional and time series data. It involves tracking the same subjects over multiple time periods, providing a rich dataset that allows for the analysis of dynamics both across subjects and over time. They are also known as *longitudinal data*. > | **ID** | **Name** | **Quarter** | **Employment Status** | |--------|----------|-------------|------------------------| | 1 | Alice | Q4 2022 | Employed | | 1 | Alice | Q1 2023 | Employed | | 1 | Alice | Q2 2023 | Unemployed | | 2 | Bob | Q4 2022 | Unemployed | | 2 | Bob | Q1 2023 | Employed | | 2 | Bob | Q2 2023 | Employed | ::: ## Benefits from using panel data Based on @hsiao2022analysis and @baltagi2008econometric: ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Heterogeneity - **Naive Model:** $$ \text{consumption}_{s} = \text{lag_consumption}_{s} + \text{price}_{s} + \text{income}_{s} + \text{error_term}_{s} $$ - **Omitted Variables:** - Variables such as education level or religion may influence both $\text{lag_consumption}_{s}$ and $\text{consumption}_{s}$. - Omitting these variables can introduce bias in estimating the effects. - **Panel Data:** - Allows tracking the same states over multiple periods. - Captures individual-specific **constant** differences between states, reducing bias from omitted unobserved variables. ### Variability **Panel data give more informative data, more variability, and more precision.** - **Compared to Time Series**: - Aggregated data often lacks individual detail - This leads to higher collinearity issues - Panel data helps reduce these issues. - **Compared to Cross-Sectional Data**: - Panel data captures variations over time that are not visible in a single cross-sectional snapshot, providing more insight into temporal dynamics. - **Compared to Repeated Cross-Sections**: - Panel data: tracks the same individuals over multiple periods - This enables control of individual-specific effects and leads to more precise estimates. ### Dynamics of adjustments > Dynamics of adjustements refer to the way in which individuals, companies or other entities react over time to a change, be it **public policy**, an **economic shock**, or some other intervention. Rather than focusing on a single point in time, adjustment dynamics explore how these reactions **evolve** and **stabilize**, or continue to **change**, after the intervention. > - **Identify Immediate and Delayed Effects**: - Track initial impacts and their evolution over time. - Assess whether effects are temporary or permanent. - **Capture Heterogeneity in Responses**: Analyze how different entities experience varying impacts. - **More Accurate Impact Assessment**: Control for unobserved heterogeneity to reduce bias / improve precision. ### Undetectable Mechanisms Panel data can reveal underlying mechanisms not detectable in pure cross-sectional or time-series data. ::: {.callout-note} ## Example Cross-Sectional Data: Shows an average labor force participation rate of 50%. However, this does not tell us if: - Each person has a 50% chance of participating in the labor force each year (high turnover), or - 50% of the population works continuously while the other 50% does not participate at all (no turnover). ::: With Panel Data you can: - **Track Individual Changes** - **Identify Hidden Patterns** ### Others Additional benefits include: - Panel data facilitate the **modeling** of complex mechanisms, for instance studying [technical efficiency](#benefits-from-using-panel-data "Technical efficiency refers to the effectiveness with which inputs are converted into outputs. In economic terms, it measures how well a firm or individual uses resources to produce goods or services."). - Micro-level data (e.g., individual or firm-level) can be **more accurate than aggregated** macro-level data, reducing biases from aggregation. - When using more advanced methods, macro-panel data have a longer time series. Thus, panel unit root tests, for example, benefit from standard asymptotic distributions, avoiding issues common in pure time-series unit root tests. ::: ## Challenges of panel data Based on @hsiao2022analysis and @baltagi2008econometric: ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Data collection - Cost and complexity - **Changes** in definitions or survey methods may produce changes in the measured variable. - Repeated errors: - In **any** data collection process, measurement errors can occur (e.g., unclear questions, memory errors, deliberate distortion of responses like prestige bias, interviewer effects). - These errors can be **repeated** over time, leading to biases when studying dynamics. - That said, when these errors are not systematic, they can sometimes be **detected** and **corrected**. In such cases, panel data also offer an advantage. - Incomplete data: data may be **missing** for certain periods, or certain populations (see "Selectivity problems") complicating the analysis. ### Selectivity problems - **Attrition**: Respondents may drop out over time, potentially introducing selection bias. - Threatens [**external validity**](#challenges-of-panel-data "The extent to which a study's results can be generalized to other populations, settings, and times.") if the dropout rate affects the representativeness of the sample relative to the true population. - Threatens [**internal validity**](#challenges-of-panel-data "The extent to which a study accurately shows a cause-and-effect relationship within the sample") if attrition is non-random and related to specific characteristics or outcomes (**endogenous attrition**). - **Nonresponse**: - Occurs when respondents refuse to participate, possibly from the first interview, or if they are unreachable (e.g., not at home, have moved, or deceased). - Similar to attrition, nonresponse can threaten both [**external validity**](#challenges-of-panel-data "The extent to which a study's results can be generalized to other populations, settings, and times.") and [**internal validity**](#challenges-of-panel-data "The extent to which a study accurately shows a cause-and-effect relationship within the sample") depending on whether the missing data is random or systematic. - For some studies, [censoring](#challenges-of-panel-data "occurs when the value of a variable is only partially known. For example, in a study of income, if we know only that a person's income is above a certain threshold but not the exact amount, the data is censored.") and [truncating](#challenges-of-panel-data "happens when data is collected only within a certain range, leading to the exclusion of observations outside that range. For example, if a study on poverty only includes individuals with incomes below a certain level, it truncates the sample by excluding those with higher incomes.") are important issues too. ### Short time-series dimension - Typical micro-panels: **short time span** for each individual. - **Asymptotic considerations**: Often rely on the number of individuals tending to infinity. - **Implication**: A sufficiently large number of individuals is necessary to maintain the reliability of statistical properties. - Panels with **longer time spans**: - **Data collection challenges**: More expensive, with higher risk of attrition. - **Computational difficulties**: Particularly with [limited dependent variable models](#challenges-of-panel-data "statistical models used when the dependent variable is limited or censored, such as models for binary data (logit, probit), or censored data (Tobit)."). ### Cross-section dependence - **Standard Models**: Assume cross-sectional independence between units. - **Reality**: In macroeconomic contexts, this assumption might not hold. For example, the reaction of country A to a public policy can impact country B, especially if they are economically connected. - Accounting for cross-section dependence turns out to be important and affect inference. - **Possible checks**: Cross-sectional dependence tests. ::: ## Let's test your understanding :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(wooldridge) library(kableExtra) data('cps78_85') rbind(head(cps78_85), tail(cps78_85)) %>% kable() %>% kable_styling(font_size = 12, full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: :::: # A reminder of the OLS model ## Simple linear model The model can be written as: $$ y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + u $$ where: - $y$: the dependent variable, - $x$: the explanatory variable, - $\beta_0$: the intercept (constant term), - $\beta_1$: the coefficient of the explanatory variable, - $u$: the error term. ## Basic idea - **Generating Data**: We assume an underlying line represents the relationship between variables. Observed data points scatter around this line due to a random error term. - **Fitting the Line**: Adjust the slope ($\beta_1$) and intercept ($\beta_0$) to minimize residuals, the distances between observed points and the estimated line. This creates the best-fit prediction model. - **Prediction**: The model predicts $y$ values based on $x$, but it’s an **approximation** of the true underlying process. - **Estimation vs True Model**: Minimizing residuals doesn't perfectly capture the true model, so we use "hat" notations ($\hat{y}$, $\hat{\beta}$) to indicate that these are estimated values. ## Illustration
## Multiple Linear Model For multiple explanatory variables, we use the **multiple linear model**, which can be written in matrix form as: $$ \underbrace{y}_{n \times 1} = \underbrace{X}_{n \times (K+1)} \underbrace{\beta}_{(K+1) \times 1} + \underbrace{\epsilon}_{n \times 1} $$ :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} $$ y = \begin{pmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_n \end{pmatrix} $$ $$ X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & x_{11} & x_{12} & \dots & x_{1k} \\ 1 & x_{21} & x_{22} & \dots & x_{2k} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 1 & x_{n1} & x_{n2} & \dots & x_{nk} \end{pmatrix} $$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} $$ \beta = \begin{pmatrix} \beta_0 \\ \beta_1 \\ \beta_2 \\ \vdots \\ \beta_k \end{pmatrix} $$ $$ \epsilon = \begin{pmatrix} \epsilon_1 \\ \epsilon_2 \\ \vdots \\ \epsilon_n \end{pmatrix} $$ ::: :::: ## Assumptions of the linear model ## Deriving the OLS estimator in the matrix form ## Proof :::{.incremental} - The objective is to minimize the sum of squares of the residuals, i.e. : - $$S(\beta) = (y - X\beta)'(y - X\beta)$$ - Let's develop this expression: - $$S(\beta) = y'y - 2\beta'X'y + \beta'X'X\beta$$ - To find the value of $\beta$ that minimizes this expression, we differentiate $S(\beta)$ with respect to $\beta$ : - $$\frac{\partial S(\beta)}{\partial \beta} = -2X'y + 2X'X\beta$$ - By setting this derivative equal to zero to minimize $S(\beta)$, we obtain the following equation: - $$X'X\hat{\beta} = X'y$$ - Solving this equation for $\hat{\beta}$ yields : - $$\hat{\beta} = (X'X)^{-1}X'y$$ ::: ## Unbiasedness of the OLS estimator ## Efficiency of the OLS estimator ## Inference / Normality of the OLS estimator ## A few words about the econometrics approach - We pose a model with assumptions to deduce properties about the estimators (absence of bias, distribution for inference). - The credibility of the assumptions is essential for confidence in the results, but may vary depending on the context and the data structure. - These assumptions need to be validated by economic intuition, statistical tests and expert discussion. - It is important to have solid reasons for accepting assumptions; they are not neutral. - Some assumptions may become less credible depending on the nature of the data (e.g. correlation in panel data). - For panel data, more sophisticated models are needed to handle correlations between repeated observations. # Repeated Cross-sectional data ## Why interest in repeated cross-sectional data - Repeated cross-sectional data are not panel data - And are therefore not discussed a lot in this course. - However, they do have a temporal dimension - They're halfway between the cross-sectional data you're used to and panel data - Knowing how to analyze them is useful, and dealing with this question will enable us to make some final recaps on the OLS regressions ## Repeated Cross-Sectional Data Over Time - **Time Dimension**: - Accounted for by adding indicator variables for each data collection period. - *Note*: Use the earliest year as the reference period. - **Increased Sample Size**: - Stacking data from multiple years boosts statistical precision. - Example: Estimate a model \( y = X\beta + u \) using data from both 2022 and 2023 - **Precision in Coefficients**: - More accurate coefficient estimates, assuming variable effects are **constant over time**. - If effects vary by period, add **time indicators** and interact them with relevant variables. ## Application 1 :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="80%"} Let's take an example from @WooldridgeJeffrey, where we track the **number of children per woman** (this will be the dependent variable $y$) between 1972 and 1984. The model includes variables such as education, age and other socio-demographic characteristics. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(wooldridge) data('fertil1') fertil1$age_square <- fertil1$age^2 reg <- lm(kids ~ educ + age + age_square + black + east + northcen + west + farm + othrural + town + smcity + y74 + y76 + y78 + y80 + y82 + y84, fertil1) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Questions 1. In this example, observations cover the period from 1972 to 1984, for even-numbered years. You'll notice that $y72$ is not included in the table. Why is $y72$ removed? 2. What can you say about changes in the number of children per woman between 1972 and 1984? ::: ::: ::: {.column width="20%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Interpretation of Coefficients: Levels vs. Logs - **Y in levels, X in levels** - Form: Y = α + βX + ε - Interpretation: 1 unit increase in X changes Y by β units. - **Y in levels, X in log** - Form: Y = α + β log(X) + ε - Interpretation: 1% increase in X changes Y by β/100 units. - **Y in log, X in levels** - Form: log(Y) = α + βX + ε - Interpretation: 1 unit increase in X changes Y by approximately β * 100 %. - **Y in log, X in log** - Form: log(Y) = α + β log(X) + ε - Interpretation: 1% increase in X changes Y by β % (elasticity). *Note*: see @WooldridgeJeffrey, section A-4b The Natural Logarithm ## Interacting Year Dummies with Variables to Capture Changing Effects - **Assumption**: In the previous model, explanatory variable effects (excluding time dummies) are assumed constant over time. - Example: Education has the same partial effect ($\beta_{educ}$) on the number of children each year. - **When Effects May Vary**: - If we suspect that effects of explanatory variables change over time, we should interact these variables with year dummies. - This approach allows testing for variations in effects across different years. **Goal**: Capture changes in variable effects across time by adding interactions between explanatory variables and year indicators. ## Application 2: Evolution of the gender wage gap and returns to education :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="80%"} \begin{align} \log(\text{lwage}) = & \ \beta_0 + \delta_0 \cdot y85 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{educ} + \delta_1 \cdot y85 \cdot \text{educ} + \beta_2 \cdot \text{exper} \\ & + \beta_3 \cdot \text{exper}^2 + \beta_4 \cdot \text{union} + \beta_5 \cdot \text{female} + \delta_5 \cdot y85 \cdot \text{female} + u \end{align} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(wooldridge) data('cps78_85') reg <- lm(lwage ~ y85 + educ + y85*educ + exper + expersq + union + female + y85*female, cps78_85) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="20%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Dependent Variable: Log Wage

(Intercept) 0.4589*** 0.093
y85 0.1178 0.124
educ 0.0747*** 0.007
exper 0.0296*** 0.004
expersq -4e-04*** 0.000
union 0.2021*** 0.030
female -0.3167*** 0.037
y85:educ 0.0185** 0.009
y85:female 0.0851* 0.051
````` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Chow Test: Assessing Joint Nullity of Coefficients - When working with repeated cross-sectional data, we may ask: - Is the model that determines wages in 1978 the same as in 1985? - Specifically, do explanatory variables (e.g., education, experience, union status, gender) have the same impact on wages in both years? - Key Question: - If we estimate separate regressions for each year, would the coefficients be the same? - Hypothesis: - Null hypothesis (H₀): The two periods follow the same regression function. - Alternative: One or more of the slopes differ across groups. - Method: - Use a **Chow Test** (a specific application of the Fisher test) to compare the two regression models and test if their coefficients are statistically different. ## Chow Test: Assessing Joint Nullity of Coefficients ::: {.panel-tabset} ### R Package ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(wooldridge) data('cps78_85') library(strucchange) # Modèle de régression model_full <- lm(lwage ~ educ + exper + union + female, data = cps78_85) # Repérer à partir de quel individu on passe aux données de 1985 # (les données des deux bases sont empilées en ligne, autrement : réordonner) # pour spécifier le point de rupture n_78 <- sum(cps78_85$year==78) n <- dim(cps78_85)[1] # Réaliser le test pour comparer les coefficients du modèle pour les deux groupes (1978 et 1985) chow_test <- sctest(lwage ~ educ + exper + union + female, type = "Chow", point = n_78/n, data = cps78_85) # Afficher les résultats du test print(chow_test) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Chow test data: lwage ~ educ + exper + union + female F = 48.443, p-value < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: ### With time indicators ::: {.panel-tabset} #### Theory \begin{align} \log(\text{wage}) &= \beta_0 + \gamma_0 y85 \\ &+ \beta_1 \text{educ} + \gamma_1 (\text{educ}\times y85) \\ &+ \beta_2 \text{exp} + \gamma_2 (\text{exp} \times y85) \\ &+ \beta_3 \text{union} + \gamma_3 (\text{union} \times y85) \\ &+ \beta_4 \text{female} + \gamma_4 (\text{female} \times y85) + u \end{align} **Constrained model**: $$ \log(\text{wage}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{educ} + \beta_2 \text{exp} + \beta_3 \text{union} + \beta_4 \text{female} + u $$ **Statistic**: $$ F = \frac{\left( \frac{\text{SCR}_{\text{contraint}} - \text{SCR}_{\text{complet}}}{q} \right)}{\left( \frac{\text{SCR}_{\text{complet}}}{n-k} \right)} $$ #### Question #### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(wooldridge) # <1> data('cps78_85') # <1> lm_compl <- lm(lwage ~ y85 + y85*(educ + exper + union + female), data = cps78_85) # <2> lm_const <- lm(lwage ~ educ + exper + union + female, data = cps78_85) # <3> SSR_compl <- sum(residuals(lm_compl)^2) # <4> SSR_const <- sum(residuals(lm_const)^2) # <5> k <- length(coef(lm_compl)) # <6> q <- length(coef(lm_compl)) - length(coef(lm_const)) # <6> n <- dim(cps78_85)[1] # <6> numerator <- (SSR_const - SSR_compl)/q # <7> denominator <- SSR_compl/(n-k) # <7> F_stat <- numerator/denominator # <7> df1 <- q # <8> df2 <- n-k # <8> p_value <- pf(F_stat, df1, df2, lower.tail = FALSE) # <9> cat("Statistic du test:", F_stat, "\n") # <10> cat("P-value:", p_value, "\n") # <10> ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Statistic du test: 48.44283 P-value: 2.795437e-45 ``` ::: ::: 1. Load the data 2. Estimate the unconstrained model 3. Estimate the constrained model 4. Compute the SSR for the unconstrained model 5. Compute the SSR for the constrained model 6. Compute the number of parameters in both models, and the number of observations 7. Compute the statistic 8. Compute the degrees of freedom 9. Compute the p-value 10. Display the results ::: ### Estimating the model on 3 samples ::: {.panel-tabset} #### Theory $$ F=\frac{\left[\mathrm{SSR}_{\text{pooled}}-\left(\mathrm{SSR}_{1978}+\mathrm{SSR}_{1985}\right)\right]}{\mathrm{SSR}_{1978}+\mathrm{SSR}_{1985}} \cdot \frac{[n-2(k+1)]}{k+1} $$ Here, only one form of the model is estimated: $$ \log(\text{wage}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{educ} + \beta_2 \text{exp} + \beta_3 \text{union} + \beta_4 \text{female} + u $$ - $\text{SSR}_\text{pooled}$ is the sum of squared residuals obtained by estimating the model on the whole sample - $\text{SSR}_{1978}$ is obtained by estimating the model on the sub-sample of individuals from the 1978 collection. - $text{SSR}_{1985}$ is obtained by estimating the model on the sub-sample of individuals from the 1985 collection. #### Question #### Code ::: {.cell class='smaller-code'} ```{.r .cell-code} library(wooldridge) # <1> data('cps78_85') # <1> data_1978 <- subset(cps78_85, year == 78) # <1> data_1985 <- subset(cps78_85, year == 85) # <1> model_formula <- lwage ~ educ + exper + union + female # <2> model_1978 <- lm(model_formula, data = data_1978) # <3> model_1985 <- lm(model_formula, data = data_1985) # <3> pooled_model <- lm(model_formula, data = cps78_85) # <4> SSR_1978 <- sum(residuals(model_1978)^2) # <5> SSR_1985 <- sum(residuals(model_1985)^2) # <5> SSR_pooled <- sum(residuals(pooled_model)^2) # <5> n1 <- nrow(data_1978) # <6> n2 <- nrow(data_1985) # <6> k <- length(coef(pooled_model)) # <6> numerator <- (SSR_pooled - (SSR_1978 + SSR_1985)) / k # <7> denominator <- (SSR_1978 + SSR_1985) / (n1 + n2 - 2*k) # <7> chow_statistic <- numerator / denominator # <7> df1 <- k # <8> df2 <- n1 + n2 - 2*k # <8> p_value <- pf(chow_statistic, df1, df2, lower.tail = FALSE) # <8> cat("Statistic du test de Chow:", chow_statistic, "\n") # <9> cat("P-value:", p_value, "\n") # <9> ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Statistic du test de Chow: 48.44283 P-value: 2.795437e-45 ``` ::: ::: 1. Load the data 2. Specify model formula 3. Estimate model on sub-samples 4. Estimate model on all data 5. Calculate SSR 6. Count the number of individuals in each subgroup and determine the number of parameters to be estimated 7. Calculate the statistic 8. Specify the degrees of freedom and deduce the p-value 9. Display test results ::: ::: ## Illustration ## Focusing on Slope Differences in the Chow Test - In the previous example, we tested if all coefficients (including intercept) were identical in the 1978 and 1985 models. - If only the intercept differed, we could still reject the null hypothesis. - Sometimes, we may want to focus only on **slope differences** (explanatory variable coefficients), ignoring the intercept. - Example: Intercept might differ due to exogenous factors like inflation, which is less relevant to our main interest in the effect of explanatory variables over time. - Solution: - Exclude the intercept from the Chow test by adjusting the procedure. - Additional Resources: - For more details on this approach and multi-period data cases, see @WooldridgeJeffrey, Section 13-1a, on the Chow test for structural changes over time. ## Conclusion - This chapter reviewed fundamental econometric concepts. - We have not yet explored **panel data**, which offer richer insights than repeated cross-sectional data. - **Panel data** allow tracking individuals over time, enabling control for *unobserved heterogeneity*. - However, **panel data** also introduce additional complexities and methodological challenges. # References ::: {#refs} :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
